meta.title: Taskflow, explained
meta.summary: A team to-do app. A Next.js web app talks to a small API, which stores tasks in Postgres and hands slow work (emails, webhooks) to a background worker.

nodes.label: Team member
nodes.summary: Someone using Taskflow in their browser.

nodes.label: Web app
nodes.summary: Pages and React components. Server components fetch data; client components handle forms and optimistic updates.

nodes.label: Auth middleware
nodes.summary: Runs before every request. Reads the session cookie, rejects anonymous users, and puts the user id on the request.

nodes.label: Tasks API
nodes.summary: Thin HTTP layer. Parses and validates input with Zod, then calls the task service. Never touches the database directly.

nodes.label: Task service
nodes.summary: All business rules live here: who can edit a task, what happens when it is completed, which events fire.

nodes.label: Billing service
nodes.summary: Checks plan limits (free teams get 50 open tasks) and syncs subscription state from Stripe webhooks.

nodes.label: Postgres
nodes.summary: The source of truth for teams, users and tasks.

nodes.label: Job queue
nodes.summary: Holds slow work so requests stay fast. Each job is retried 5 times with backoff.

nodes.label: Worker
nodes.summary: Pulls jobs off the queue: sends emails, fires customer webhooks, rolls up daily stats.

flows.title: Create a task
flows.summary: The most common write in the app. Follow it from the click to the email the assignee receives.

steps.label: Types a title, presses Add
steps.detail: The form is a client component. It shows the task instantly (optimistic update) before the server answers.

steps.label: POST /api/tasks
steps.detail: A normal fetch with the session cookie attached. The auth middleware runs first: no valid session means a 401 and the request stops.
steps.why: Doing auth once in middleware means no route can forget to check it.

steps.label: Validates, calls createTask()
steps.detail: Zod rejects bad input with a 422 before any business logic runs.

steps.label: Checks the plan limit
steps.detail: Free teams can have 50 open tasks. Over the limit, billing.checkLimit() throws and the API answers 402.

steps.label: INSERT the task
steps.detail: Inside a transaction together with an activity-log row, so the history can never miss a task.

steps.label: Enqueue “task.assigned”
steps.detail: Only if someone else was assigned. The request does not wait for the email.
steps.why: Email providers can take seconds. Queuing keeps the click under 100 ms.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: The real task replaces the optimistic one. If anything failed, the form rolls back and shows the error.

steps.label: Worker sends the email
steps.detail: Usually within a second. Failed jobs retry with backoff, then the assignee gets the email.

flows.title: Upgrade to Pro
flows.summary: Payment happens on Stripe’s page. We only learn about it through a webhook.

steps.label: checkout.session.completed
steps.detail: The webhook route checks the Stripe signature first, then hands the event to the billing service.
steps.why: Without the signature check, anyone could POST a fake ‘paid’ event.

steps.label: Set team.plan = 'pro'
steps.detail: Idempotent: replaying the same event changes nothing.

changes.title: Move task emails onto the queue
changes.author: claude-agent
changes.what: createTask() used to call Resend inline. Now it enqueues a job and the worker sends it.
changes.why: p95 for POST /api/tasks was 1.8 s because of email latency. It is now 90 ms.
changes.risk: Emails can arrive a few seconds late; retries may duplicate an email if the provider times out after sending.

changes.title: Enforce the 50-task limit on the free plan
changes.author: maria
changes.what: New billing.checkLimit() call before every insert, plus a 402 response and an upgrade banner.
changes.why: Pricing change agreed for Q4: free stays useful for small teams, heavy users upgrade.

changes.title: Verify Stripe webhook signatures
changes.author: security-agent
changes.what: The webhook route now rejects any request whose Stripe-Signature header does not verify.
changes.why: An audit found the endpoint trusted any POST. Anyone could have upgraded a team for free.

changes.title: Split auth checks out of route handlers
changes.author: dev-agent-2
changes.what: Twelve copies of the session check were replaced by one middleware.
changes.why: Two new routes had shipped without auth. One place to check means none can forget.

concepts.title: Routes are thin, the service is thick
concepts.body: API routes only parse input and shape the response. Every rule lives in packages/core: limits, permissions, side effects.
concepts.analogy: Routes are the waiter: they take the order and bring the plate. The service is the kitchen.

concepts.title: Slow things go on the queue
concepts.body: If something talks to the outside world and the user does not need the result right now, it becomes a job.
concepts.analogy: Like dropping a letter in a postbox instead of walking it to the recipient.

concepts.title: Optimistic UI
concepts.body: The web app shows your change before the server confirms it, then quietly fixes things up if the server disagrees.

quiz.question: You need to add a rule: “archived teams can’t create tasks”. Where does it go?
quiz.explain: Business rules belong in the service, so every caller gets them: API, worker and scripts.

quiz.question: Why doesn’t creating a task wait for the email to send?
options: Emails are sent by the browser
The email is queued and the worker sends it later
Emails are only sent on Pro plans
quiz.explain: PR #482 moved emails onto the queue, which cut p95 from 1.8 s to 90 ms.

quiz.question: What stops someone faking a Stripe ‘payment succeeded’ event?
quiz.explain: Added in #475 after an audit. The middleware doesn’t run for Stripe, because Stripe has no session cookie.
